articles.title: Unmasking misogyny: How a Malayalam YouTube channel weaponises science against women
articles.summary: In July 2026, during a debate on 24 News’ Thammil Thammil about whether women should face restrictions on what they wear, a woman panellist posed a question that cut to the heart of the argument: If women’s clothes provoke sexual assault, what explains the rape of children and elderly women? Muhammed Ameer, an ‘educator’ and one of the prominent faces of the Malayalam digital platform Unmasking Anomalies (UA), had an answer. “Consider”, he said, “the amount of sexual imagery men are exposed to every day, from hoardings and advertisements to models.” A man sees a sexually exposed woman and becomes sexually frustrated. Just as someone who cannot shout back at a boss might take their anger out on someone at home, he argued, sexual frustration can be taken out on a different target. This, Ameer said, was “frustration-aggression theory”. When another panellist objected that this did not explain why women should change what they wear, Ameer was emphatic. “This is a psychological theory,” he asserted. “It’s not me saying this.” It is an effective way to make an argument, enough to make the person sitting across from you in a debate pause and reconsider what they can immediately challenge. Once a claim is attached to a psychological theory or a scientific study, it can easily begin to sound like a ‘fact’ rather than an opinion. The reaction in the comments under the video shows how deceptively powerful this method is. “The UA team never goes wrong wherever they participate. They have done thorough research,” one viewer wrote. Another described the women on the panel as “a group of ladies devoid of even the slightest trace of intelligence or awareness.” The women, after all, could not respond well enough to the ‘science’ being cited. But what happens when you follow that science back to its sources, and the argument doesn’t stand anymore? We will return to why Ameer’s claim does not hold up. But first, a little about the channel he represents. Unmasking Anomalies, formerly known as Unmasking Atheism, is an Islamic theological group, primarily known for its debates and arguments with atheist and ex-Muslim critics. But it has a second speciality. The channel’s main figures — Abdulla Basil CP, Muhammed Ameer, CP Abdu Samad, Hilal Saleem, and others — can be frequently seen refereeing debates about feminism, women’s clothing, and queer lives, using the vocabulary of psychology, neuroscience, evolutionary biology, and even feminist scholarship. It is this strand of the channel’s work that we are setting out to examine here. We watched and analysed six primary videos and several shorter videos from UA, tracing their citations back to the original sources wherever available. When the research did not appear to support the conclusions drawn from it, we examined the studies, their methods, limitations, and caveats. The channel’s approach bears resemblance to what is called the “scientific blackpill” in parts of the manosphere: cherry-picking research to make sweeping claims about how men and women are wired and how they should behave. This is not to say UA is simply a blackpill platform. Its hosts have repeatedly stated that men are responsible for sexual assault regardless of what a woman wears, while many who adhere to the scientific blackpill tend to place the blame squarely on women. This bare-minimum position, however, does not undo the larger pattern in UA’s videos. The channel’s speakers move easily from psychologists and criminologists like Neil Malamuth and Adam Lankford to feminist scholars such as Sheila Jeffreys and Sandra Lee Bartky, often selectively quoting or misrepresenting their work to arrive at conclusions that can ultimately be boiled down to: ‘science says women should stay at home and cover themselves.’ So, for this story, we followed the citations back to the source and asked a simple question: does the research actually say what UA says it says? The ‘sexual frustration’ theory The debate over sexual frustration is a useful place to begin, both because it illustrates UA’s method particularly clearly and because the exchange became one of the channel’s more widely viewed moments. But follow Ameer’s argument back to the research he cites, and his claims begin to look considerably less certain. The frustration-aggression hypothesis, first proposed in 1939, is indeed a longstanding psychological theory, but it is not a theory of sexual frustration. In fact, the source Ameer is drawing on, as he has stated in later videos, is criminologist Adam Lankford’s 2021 paper, A Sexual Frustration Theory of Aggression, Violence, and Crime . Now, there is an important distinction here between proposing a theory and having evidence that establishes the theory. Lankford’s work, which TNM read through in detail, is a review and theoretical paper. It draws on other studies, including the frustration-aggression theory, to propose a possible relationship between sexual frustration and aggression, while calling for further research. It does not present any empirical research of its own to back this theory. Lankford is also clearly not establishing, at any point, that exposure to sexualised images can cause sexual frustration to build up, that this frustration is then displaced onto another person, or that women’s clothing has any demonstrated effect on rape. Read the paper here . In fact, right in the introduction, Lankford rejects the old “dam-bursting” model of male sexuality — the idea that sexual pressure builds up over time and eventually has to be released somewhere. This model, he says, “misrepresents how the male body functions” and “ignores psychological and qualitative dimensions of sexual frustration,” among other problems. More importantly, he warns that because most crimes are committed by men, embracing the “dam-bursting” view could be seen as “excusing males based on their biology or blaming females for failing to please them.” Either, he writes, would be “highly offensive”. The problems with Ameer’s argument had not gone unnoticed. The video drew responses from feminist activists, influencers, and psychologists, who questioned the way scientific research was being used to explain sexual violence and defend restrictions on women. Among those who took note was Darsana Varier, a sociology researcher and feminist. The Thammil Thammil clip had left Darsana both intrigued and sceptical. Her own interest lay in studying gendered behaviour from a sociological perspective, and she wanted to understand what criminological and psychological research had to say on the subject. Muhammed Ameer speaking during the debate on women’s clothing restrictions on 24 News’ Thammil Thammil. “The first time we all heard about the frustration-aggression hypothesis was on Thammil Thammil when he cited it. But it sounded suspicious to me that a study would validate this relationship between sexual assault and clothing of victims, much less the claim that this relationship would result in increased assaults on children and the elderly,” she told TNM. “But of course, if studies were being done and published to explore this relationship, that would be kind of a huge finding for us.” So she decided to read Lankford’s paper, and realised the problem. “UA’s primary citation (which is the Lankford paper) treats its own claim as an open question,” she said. In the paper, Lankford asks whether an increasingly sexualised American culture will lead to more sexual frustration or less, and what effects online pornography, masturbation, prostitution, and conjugal visits might have on short- and long-term sexual frustration. These are questions he identifies as requiring further research, not findings he claims to have established. Yet Ameer had presented the idea as an established psychological explanation for sexual assault. “That’s when I realised their entire argument was standing on shaky grounds.” The issue came up again when Darsana debated Ameer on the UA channel. Ameer doubled down on his Lankford citation to reiterate his position that sexualised imagery could cause frustration in men, which could in turn lead to assaults on women, children, and elderly people. He specifically quoted these lines from the paper: “Research has found that under similar conditions (of sexual arousal), men express significantly more interest in engaging in kinky sexual behavior; in having sex with children or the elderly; and in being willing to use money, lies, alcohol, drugs, or coercion to get someone to have sex with them.” But yet again, there is a problem with this argument. The source that Lankford uses to make this point is Dan Ariely and George Loewenstein’s 2005 study, The Heat of the Moment . The experiment involved just 35 male undergraduates at UC Berkeley, a university in California. Participants were asked to bring themselves to a state of high sexual arousal through self-stimulation (masturbation) at home and then rate a series of hypothetical statements on a scale of 0 to 100. One of the questions was whether participants could imagine being attracted to a 12-year-old girl. When participants were sexually aroused after self-stimulation, that is, in the “heat of the moment”, the average score increased. But to be clear, that is not the same as asking whether they would sexually assault a child. The question was about “imagined attraction,” not willingness to commit sexual violence. Besides, the responses were hypothetical and self-reported. The researchers explicitly acknowledged in the paper that they could not know how accurately the answers predicted real-world behaviour. There are, then, several steps between this experiment and the claims being made by the UA channel. The chain goes something like this: A small study of 35 male students measures responses to hypothetical questions under induced sexual arousal. Lankford then uses it in a theoretical paper about how sexual frustration might contribute to aggression and crime, while also making clear that sexual frustration is not, by itself, a sufficient explanation for violence. UA, in turn, presents the broader argument as a “psychological theory” to explain why children and elderly women might be raped by sexually frustrated men, and uses it in a debate about regulating women's clothing. The problem, as Darsana points out, was not simply that a study had been cited incorrectly, but that a new causal link was being inserted between what the study actually measured and the conclusion UA wanted to reach. “If you want to draw a clear causal line between sexual harassment and clothing choices,” she told TNM, “that needs to be explicitly mentioned in whatever study you’re quoting.” The viral “frustration-aggression” clip had brought UA significant backlash, following which Ameer and Samad, a clinical psychologist by profession, released a video defending their ‘science’. One of the arguments made in the video was that “feminists just want to keep saying that rapes happen. They do not want to acknowledge or address the root causes.” That claim, too, is difficult to square when you consider the history of the feminist anti-rape movement. Unmasking Anomalies speakers Samad (left), a clinical psychologist, and Muhammed Ameer (right), in a video defending the channel’s use of scientific research following backlash over Ameer’s comments on the “frustration-aggression” theory. Feminist activists did not simply ‘document’ rape. For decades, they have tried to understand why sexual violence happens, the social and institutional conditions that enable it, and what can be done to prevent it. Historian Catherine O Jacquet’s account of the feminist anti-rape movement describes how women’s liberation activists challenged the idea of rape as an isolated individual act. They developed a feminist analysis that connected sexual violence to gender inequality and male power, while also challenging rape culture and victim-blaming, demanding that survivors be heard and believed, and pushing for changes to rape laws and medical practices. Rose Corrigan’s history of the movement extensively documents how feminist activists helped establish rape crisis centres, provided support to survivors, and campaigned for legal reform. In India, too, feminist activism has challenged not just the occurrence of sexual violence but the assumptions, laws, and institutions that shape how it is understood and addressed. One defining moment, for instance, came in the Mathura custodial rape case, after the Supreme Court acquitted two policemen accused of raping a young Adivasi woman in custody. Four law teachers — Upendra Baxi, Lotika Sarkar, Vasudha Dhagamwar, and Raghunath Kelkar — subsequently wrote an open letter in 1979 challenging the judgement’s assumptions about consent, resistance, and Mathura’s sexual history. The letter helped galvanise a nationwide feminist anti-rape campaign that contributed to the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1983, which introduced important changes to rape law, including provisions addressing custodial rape. Another example is the Justice Verma Committee, constituted in the wake of the December 2012 Delhi gang rape following sustained public and feminist pressure. Its report examined sexual violence as an expression of power and recommended changes to criminal law. Indian feminist scholarship has also examined the social beliefs used to blame women for sexual violence. Among these, for instance, is a 2019 study in which researchers Lipi Begum and Ravinder Barn explored how women’s clothing choices in Delhi and Mumbai were entangled with ideas about respectability, “Western” dress, and victim-blaming. These are just a handful of examples of feminists asking precisely the questions Ameer and Samad allege they are unwilling to ask: why does sexual violence happen, what social and institutional conditions sustain it, who is held responsible, and what can be done to prevent it? ‘I am a biology teacher, don't deny science’ A few months before the ‘sexual frustration theory’ episode, Abdulla Basil CP, who is a dentist by profession and one of UA’s primary speakers, had appeared on 24 News’ Thammil Thammil for another discussion, titled ‘Are beauty pageants leading people astray?’ Highlights from the March 2026 debate have since become UA’s single most-viewed video, with nearly eight lakh views as of publication. Abdulla Basil CP, a dentist by profession and one of Unmasking Anomalies’ primary speakers, during the March 2026 episode of 24 News’ Thammil Thammil on beauty pageants and women’s clothing. When the ‘debate’ inevitably reached the point of policing women’s clothing, Basil, as UA does, approached the topic through the lens of ‘biology’ and ‘neuroscience’. His argument began with a relatively straightforward observation about sexual attraction and responses to sexual stimuli before quickly moving to claims along the lines of ‘men have sexual thoughts, so women should cover up’. This was another pattern Darsana said she noticed when she went back to the studies UA cited — a problem of validity, that is, whether a study is actually measuring the thing being claimed. In several cases, she told TNM, studies examining how observers perceive women in sexualised clothing were being discussed as though they measured the likelihood of sexual assault. “They do not. A study can tell us that an observer is more likely to judge a woman in a particular way without telling us that the woman’s clothing makes sexual violence more likely.” Basil, for instance, pointed to research based on functional MRI scans , which showed that when men see a naked woman’s body, the postcentral gyrus and other areas involved in object recognition become active. This, he argued, is evidence that men see naked women as “just an object”. This, however, is not the case with women, he said, citing the argument that men and women respond differently to sexual images . From there, he arrived at a more familiar conclusion that patriarchy has peddled for years: because some men have poor impulse control, women’s exposed bodies can face “consequences”, and clothing restrictions can therefore become a biology-based form of protection. He invoked convicted sex offender Govindachamy as an example of the kind of man he had in mind. Govindachamy was convicted of sexually assaulting 23-year-old Soumya, who was later thrown from a moving train in Kerala in 2011. When other panellists on the debate challenged his argument, Basil, who is also a biology teacher, repeatedly had a simple response: “This is science, don’t deny science.” A file photograph of Govindachamy, the man convicted of sexually assaulting Soumya in the 2011 case in Kerala. But there is a much simpler distinction, hinged on basic biology, that gets lost in this discussion. People can be aroused by sexually stimulating material. They can have sexual thoughts about other people. They can find other people attractive or experience an involuntary sexual response to someone’s body. None of those things, by themselves, is a sexual transgression. Arousal is a feeling, while sexual assault is a choice to violate another person’s autonomy. The distance between the two is precisely where consent, self-control, empathy, and accountability come in, and no brain scan can turn one into the other. This ‘confusion’ became almost comical when Basil later issued an open “lie detector” challenge to people who had made videos criticising UA. The platform put out a reel calling on “male feminists” to take a lie-detector test to prove that they did not experience sexual desire when they saw “barely clothed” women. “This is not about the women who made videos against us,” Basil clarified. Women, he suggested, might deny having such thoughts because they experience sexual stimulation differently from men, or even out of “ignorance”. That is, if a woman rejected his ‘scientific accounts’, she simply did not know any better. Male feminists, Basil suggested, were a different matter. They were “foxes” who were “definitely lying”, he said, because they knew that men experience sexual thoughts when they see women in revealing clothes. So, he proposed, “let’s find out who is lying.” There was, however, a rather obvious problem with the premise. The men criticising UA were not saying that men never experience sexual thoughts. They were making the much more banal point that experiencing a sexual thought does not mean a man is entitled to act on it, stare at a woman, harass her, or assault her. Many of them also responded with videos pointing that out, displaying little interest in the ‘lie-detector test’. UA nevertheless followed up with another ‘results’ video, treating the exchange as though it had somehow exposed its critics as dishonest. Unmasking Anomalies speakers in a video claiming that male feminists, such as influencer Mallu Analyst (featured in the image), backed out of a proposed lie-detector test. Incidentally, some of Basil’s own statements in the Thammil Thammil debate provide a useful test of this claim. When a speaker on the panel asked Basil about a male oncologist examining a woman’s breast or about a man trying to rescue a female friend who is drowning while wearing little clothing, Basil did not say that the man must respond sexually simply because he can see a woman’s body. Instead, he talked about context. A doctor examining a patient, or someone helping an injured person, activates different responses in the brain, he said. So clearly, the same body can be perceived differently depending on the situation, the relationship, and what the person is doing. Basil eventually conceded the larger point himself. “Human beings have free will and intelligence,” he said. “We are not animals.” Experiencing sexual desire, he acknowledged, does not mean someone will immediately act on it. Biology is not the only factor involved; psychology matters too. That should make the leap to placing restrictions on women’s clothing harder. If sexual arousal is an involuntary response, but behaviour is shaped by context, psychology, social learning, and individual choice, then the existence of the response cannot by itself tell us what a woman should wear. It certainly cannot establish that her clothing is responsible for what another person chooses to do. Basil’s answer to this was essentially that society is not utopian. Even if most men can control themselves, he argued, there would always be people like Govindachamy who cannot or will not. He explicitly stated that women’s actions do not give men a licence to do whatever they want, and that men must be taught to exercise control. But he then added that, because such men exist, women need “protection” through more clothing. So, even while acknowledging that men are responsible for their actions, Basil’s argument ultimately places the burden of preventing sexual violence on women — by restricting what they wear. Are women’s clothes the problem or perpetrators’ attitude? Elsewhere in the same debate, Basil claimed at one point: “There is a scientific study conducted specifically among men, which found that 35% of men are potential rapists... in such a society, there needs to be a minimum level of protection.” The 35% figure comes from Neil Malamuth’s 1981 paper in the Journal of Social Issues, Rape Proclivity Among Males , which is one of the foundational texts in the scientific literature on sexual aggression. But the paper says something considerably more careful, and more interesting, than “35% of men are potential rapists.” One of the notable limitations of Malamuth’s study is its sample. The participants were predominantly male college students from the Los Angeles, Stanford, and Winnipeg areas in the US — hardly a representative sample of men in general, let alone men in Kerala in 2026. That does not make the findings scientifically meaningless, but it does complicate the number cited. In the study, the men were asked a hypothetical question: how likely would you personally be to rape a woman if you knew you would not be caught or punished? They were asked to answer on a five-point scale, ranging from 1 (not likely) to 5 (highly likely). The much-cited 35% figure refers to everyone who chose 2 or higher, which included anyone who indicated at least “some likelihood” of committing rape under those hypothetical conditions. A smaller group, about 20%, chose 3 or higher, indicating a higher likelihood. Malamuth himself is cautious about what the measure can tell us. “The hypothetical nature of this question,” he writes, “makes it difficult to judge whether it reveals any socially meaningful information.” There is an even more striking problem with the way the figure is presented by Basil. Elsewhere in the paper, Malamuth directly rejects the idea that men can be described as “potential rapists”, which is precisely the language Basil later uses while citing the study. Malamuth argues that such a category is not scientifically precise because people have “the potential to engage in virtually any behaviour”. What matters scientifically, he says, is the relative probability that different individuals would engage in a particular act under particular conditions. That is why Malamuth defines “rape proclivity” as how likely a person might be to rape under particular hypothetical circumstances, rather than treating “potential rapist” as a fixed category. The paper Basil cited, then, does not say “35% of men are potential rapists.” It says that about 35% of mostly college-student participants in the USA indicated “some likelihood” of rape when asked to imagine they could do so without being caught or punished. Basil, essentially, was taking a conditional, hypothetical measure that Malamuth himself says needs further validation, and turning it into a categorical and damning statement about men. He then used that statement to argue that, because such men exist, women need “protection” through their clothing. What the paper points to is a different, and arguably more useful, way of understanding the risk of sexual violence — one that shifts the focus from women’s clothing to men’s attitudes towards rape. Malamuth notes that, across the studies he reviewed, men with higher “rape likelihood” scores were found to be more likely to endorse what researchers call “rape myths”. So what are rape myths? The term refers to false or prejudicial beliefs about sexual assault — beliefs that can place the blame on the survivor, excuse the perpetrator, or minimise the violence itself. As psychologist Julia O’Connor notes in her research, these can include the idea that women who dress a certain way, drink alcohol, or are perceived as “promiscuous” are somehow responsible for being raped. Other rape myths excuse perpetrators by suggesting that they could not control themselves or that alcohol was responsible for their actions, while some minimise sexual assault by suggesting that an incident was not violent or serious enough to count as “real rape”. To be clear, endorsing rape myths, including the belief that women’s clothing can cause rape , can give perpetrators a way to rationalise their actions by shifting responsibility onto survivors. Such beliefs can also weaken the social norms that prohibit sexual violence, making it easier to excuse or justify harm rather than hold perpetrators accountable. So when people sit on TV debates and recycle the idea that women need to cover up to prevent rape, they are essentially reproducing a familiar rape myth. And in turn, they are influencing other men. They are also helping shift responsibility from the person who commits the violence to the person who is expected to prevent it. Though presented as rape prevention, that very argument reinforces rape culture . When rape becomes biology There is another strand of research the channel cites that is particularly relevant here — evolutionary explanations of rape. In his debate with Darsana, Ameer extensively discussed the 2000 book A Natural History of Rape: Biological Bases of Sexual Coercion , by evolutionary biologist Randy Thornhill and anthropologist Craig Palmer. He claimed the authors argued women are most likely to be raped in the age range where they are “most sexually attractive” from an evolutionary perspective. “That median age is about 15. Most women are raped between the ages of 12–25, because women are more attractive in that age range,” he stated. Ameer then questioned, “So if women are more likely to be raped at a time when they are more sexually attractive, doesn't that mean female attractiveness affects men sexually?” Darsana Varier (top left) and Muhammed Ameer (bottom) during a debate on the Unmasking Anomalies YouTube channel. There is a kernel of the book’s argument here, though whether female attractiveness can affect men sexually was never the question; that is hardly a revelation. The question is whether that can explain rape, and whether the evidence supports the leap from sexual attraction to sexual violence. Ameer’s question makes the first sound like an answer to the second, when it clearly isn’t. To be clear, Thornhill and Palmer did argue that the ages of rape victims could offer clues to how rape evolved. They cited one national dataset in which women aged 16–24 had the highest rates of rape, followed by those aged 12–15. Another study they discussed found the median age of female rape victims to be 21. The authors interpreted these patterns through an evolutionary lens. They linked women’s attractiveness to their “reproductive potential” or “fertility peak”, and proposed that rape may be linked to inherited traits that increased reproductive success among our ancestors. They argued that the ages at which women were most frequently victimised could help explain the evolutionary origins of rape. It is to be noted, however, that this is the authors’ interpretation of the data, and not a conclusion that the age figures establish on their own. Ameer also cited the book’s discussion of physical and structural barriers, including “holding teenage boys’ and girls’ camps at opposite ends of a lake so that they don’t see each other,” as a solution to prevent rape. He added, “These aren’t people who wrote a book after studying in some madrasa in Afghanistan. They were researchers. The book is written by an anthropologist and an evolutionary biologist.” The authors’ credentials, however, do not make their conclusions immune to scrutiny. A Natural History of Rape has been heavily contested by researchers across several fields, including evolutionary psychology itself, and not just by feminist scholars. The key question is whether the authors’ specific explanation of rape is actually supported by sufficient evidence. In a 2002 paper, psychologists Tony Ward and Richard Siegert challenged the theory, pointing out that Thornhill and Palmer were unable to show that their evolutionary explanation was better supported than other explanations rooted in social and cultural factors. Though they did not completely rule out a role for biology in sexual aggression, Ward and Siegert argued that there were too many unanswered questions about how such behaviour might have evolved, and how social and cultural influences shape it, to conclude that evolution alone could explain rape. ( Read the paper here .) A 2003 review by psychologist Arnold S Kahn, Rape is not a Natural Act , similarly challenged the tendency to treat rape as something that can simply be understood as a natural or biological behaviour. A more detailed 2009 critique in the Journal of Social Philosophy, Rape, Evolution, and Pseudoscience , raised further objections to the book’s arguments, including its treatment of rape as a universal feature of human societies, which in turn lends the act an air of inevitability. The authors drew on anthropologist Peggy Reeves Sanday’s cross-cultural research (1981), which found substantial variation in the prevalence and social meaning of rape. In her study of 156 societies, Sanday classified 47% as “rape-free” — meaning rape was either extremely infrequent or did not occur. She also found that higher rates of rape were associated with broader cultural patterns, including interpersonal violence and male dominance. In some societies, rape functioned as punishment, a threat, or a means of controlling women. ( Read Sanday’s study .) This complicates claims that rape is an evolutionary reproductive strategy rooted in male biology and underscores the importance of examining the social and cultural conditions in which sexual violence occurs. It is also notable that A Natural History of Rape has had a second life in the red-pill and incel internet, where its central thesis — that rape is an evolved reproductive strategy — has been extensively used by misogynistic communities to rationalise sexual violence against women. This is the “scientific blackpill” we referred to earlier: scientific research, stripped of its context and uncertainties, repurposed to make claims about what men and women are supposedly biologically destined to do. A 2024 study on incel culture explicitly states how these communities “appropriate scientific studies in genetics and evolutionary psychology to argue that women enjoy and desire sexual assault.” Ameer, here, had invoked Thornhill and Palmer as a scientific authority for claims about rape, sexual attraction, and biology, and ultimately to argue for regulating interactions between men and women and policing what women wear. But a highly contested evolutionary hypothesis cannot, by itself, become a rule for how women should live. What do women want? A consistent pattern across UA’s arguments is a deep suspicion of female sexual agency. The channel’s hosts, at least in the videos we watched, did not explicitly claim that women have no sexual feelings or desires. But they exhibited a visible habit of treating women’s stated preferences, choices, and even happiness as suspect data that can’t be trusted at face value. Men’s “impulses”, meanwhile, were presented as biological facts that society must accommodate. It was particularly striking that UA often made this argument by borrowing from feminist scholarship, oftentimes selectively, and in ways that flatten or misrepresent what the original author was actually arguing. They then used this citation as a kind of ‘gotcha’ against feminists they debated. Basil did this most clearly when he cited radical feminist scholar Sheila Jeffreys’ book The Industrial Vagina: The Political Economy of the Global Sex Trade , during his Thammil Thammil debate, to state that “billions of dollars flow into the fashion industry” to sexualise women’s bodies. “It’s not me saying this. It is people like radical feminist Sheila Jeffreys,” he said, repeating again and again, “This is not my argument. This is said by a radical feminist.” Basil cites Sheila Jeffreys’ book The Industrial Vagina: The Political Economy of the Global Sex Trade during a discussion on 24 News’ Thammil Thammil. Indeed, feminist scholars, including Gloria Steinem and Sheila Jeffreys, have extensively criticised the commercial sexualisation and objectification of women’s bodies, and there is substantial research on the way commercial culture can turn women’s bodies into commodities. The problem is what happens when that critique is lifted from its original context and made to do much more work than the source itself does. Jeffreys’ book, as its title makes clear, is about the global sex trade. It examines pornography, strip clubs, escort agencies, military prostitution, trafficking, and sex tourism, and argues that the sex trade has developed into a vast commercial industry that reinforces women’s subordination. Jeffreys does discuss the ways in which the aesthetics and practices of the sex industry can seep into mainstream culture, including fashion, music, and entertainment. But fashion is not same as or synonymous with the sex trade, as Basil seemed to conflate. Jeffreys’ argument about the commodification of women’s bodies in the sex industry also cannot simply be transplanted onto every woman who wears revealing clothes, works in fashion, or chooses to present herself in a sexualised way. The fact that feminist scholarship critiques one form of commercial sexualisation does not, by itself, establish that women’s individual choices are evidence of false consciousness, male coercion, or a need for greater restrictions on what they wear. Ameer, too, made a similar move during his appearance at Thammil Thammil , where he invoked feminist philosopher Sandra Lee Bartky, referring to her book Femininity and Domination: Studies in the Phenomenology of Oppression . Bartky’s book is a sustained examination of how patriarchal ideas about femininity become embedded in women’s everyday lives, including through expectations about their bodies, appearance, and behaviour. Ameer’s argument was that when women say their clothes are their own choice, that choice may itself have been shaped by the male gaze and patriarchal expectations. He invoked the idea of an “illusion of choice”, which is a formulation UA has returned to several times, particularly in its combative street interviews. Muhammed Ameer invokes feminist philosopher Sandra Lee Bartky’s work on the “illusion of choice” during his appearance on 24 News’ Thammil Thammil. Once again, the underlying feminist argument here is a serious one. Social pressures do not stop being social pressures simply because people experience the resulting behaviour as voluntary. Bartky, for instance, writes about how ideals of femininity become internalised and reproduced through women’s own relationships with their bodies. In the videos we watched, however, UA’s scepticism about whether a woman’s choices are truly her own appears, almost exclusively, when she chooses something the channel disapproves of. A woman who says she wants to dress a certain way may be told that she has merely internalised the male gaze. But the same suspicion does not appear when a woman says she rejects feminism, wants to be a homemaker, prefers traditional gender roles, or agrees with UA’s own arguments. In those cases, her choice is, at least in the videos we watched, treated as an authentic expression of free will. This became particularly revealing in UA’s video titled Women are saying – we don’t need feminism , where Ameer and Samad respond to a series of anti-feminist social media clips. In one clip, endorsed by the duo on air as “a great point”, a blurred woman can be seen arguing that men operate on a 24-hour cycle while women operate on a monthly one, and that expecting women to work and compete “like men” ignores their biological nature. The underlying biology is real — humans of every sex have circadian rhythms, and many women have menstrual cycles that average around 28 days. But this framing manufactures a clean binary that doesn’t stand up to actual research. The menstrual cycle varies enormously between individuals and doesn’t apply to pre-menarche or post-menopausal women, to many people on hormonal contraception, or to trans men and some non-binary people who menstruate. Meanwhile everyone, regardless of sex, has a circadian rhythm. There is another way to look at the same problem. If people’s bodies, energy levels, health, sleep, caregiving responsibilities, and personal circumstances differ, why should the answer be to tell women they are not built for the world of work? Why not ask why the world of work is built the way it is in the first place? It is established that capitalism has largely organised work around productivity, efficiency, and the demands of the employer, rather than around the messy realities of human bodies and lives. But the answer to that problem does not have to be taking women out of the workplace. It can be asking how workplaces themselves can become more humane and accommodating — for women, men, and anyone whose life does not fit neatly into a 9-to-5 template. Which woman’s choice matters more? A second clip in the same video featured American ‘tradwife’ influencer Savanna Stone, whose face is also blurred, arguing that studies show married women with children are the happiest and invoking the “paradox of declining female happiness”. Again, there is a real study behind the claim . Economists Betsey Stevenson and Justin Wolfers wrote in 2009 about a long-term decline in women’s self-reported happiness in several industrialised countries, including a decline relative to men’s happiness, despite objective gains in income, rights, and opportunity. But the crucial catch here is that while the study describes the decline, it does not establish why it happened. The authors do not conclude that feminism, women’s employment, or being single caused women to become less happy. There are many possible explanations. Feminist researchers, for instance, have pointed to the “second shift” : women entering paid employment without being able to share the domestic workload of unpaid cooking, cleaning, childcare, and other work at home. Others have looked at workplaces that still assume the ideal worker has few responsibilities outside the job, leaving people, particularly women, trying to meet the demands of both work and family. These explanations point to the conditions under which women entered the workforce and to the persistence of unequal divisions of labour, rather than establishing that feminism itself made women unhappy. There’s a further irony UA leaves for its audience to miss entirely, especially by blurring out Savanna Stone’s face in the video. (To be clear, the blurring isn’t specific to Stone, but seemingly any woman who hasn’t consented to appear in the video.) The ‘trad wife’ aesthetic in India: Why it’s more political than personal Stone, a ‘trad wife influencer’ is a highly controversial figure who has publicly advocated for women’s right-to-vote being taken away, instead batting for a ‘one family, one vote’ model with the husband having the final say. She has also built a substantial public platform and makes a living through content creation, which is precisely the kind of professional independence that her arguments suggest women should be less interested in pursuing. American ‘tradwife’ influencer Savanna Stone speaks during a podcast interview. Stone has argued that women are happiest as wives and mothers, and has publicly advocated replacing women's right to vote with a ‘one family, one vote’ system. Most significantly, journalist Ben Zand’s investigative documentary series Human uncovered a financial link between Stone and a millionaire who allegedly helped build misogynist influencer Andrew Tate’s War Room — a private network built around Tate’s worldview on masculinity, women and male dominance, and which has faced allegations of exploiting women. For the uninitiated, Tate is one of the most prominent figures in the global manosphere, a sprawling online ecosystem built around ideas about male dominance, women’s subordination, and sexual entitlement. TNM had earlier reported on how this ecosystem is increasingly not confined to the internet’s Western fringes, having found audiences, influencers, and localised versions in India, reaching boys as young as eight or nine. Inside the manosphere luring young Indian men and boys So, the woman UA presents as an example of “what women supposedly want” is someone operating within the financial ecosystem of one of the internet’s most influential anti-women movements. This same selective approach to agency extends beyond women’s roles and into UA’s arguments about queer people as well. The biology of ‘normalisation’ A September 2025 video on UA's channel, featuring Basil and Dr Hilal Saleem MBBS, talks about a controversy involving a lesbian couple on the reality TV show Bigg Boss Malayalam , and offers yet another example of the same method. Here, the question is whether queer identities and relationships should be accepted as legitimate in the first place. The controversy began after contestants Ved Lakshmi and Mastani made disparaging remarks about a lesbian couple who participated in the show, Adhila Nasarin and Fathima Noora. Lakshmi said they would not welcome the couple into their homes and objected to what they described as the “normalising” of LGBTQIA+ culture. Host Mohanlal intervened during the episode, defending the couple’s dignity and making clear that disrespect towards them would not be tolerated. He also said he would be happy to welcome Adhila and Noora into his own home and warned that contestants could face consequences for discriminatory behaviour. Thumbnail for a UA video featuring Basil and Dr Hilal Saleem, discussing the controversy over a lesbian couple’s participation in Bigg Boss Malayalam in September 2025. UA’s response, meanwhile, was to take this relatively straightforward question of dignity and inclusion and turn it into a much broader claim about the “pushing” of an “LGBTQIA+ agenda.” Basil argued that Lakshmi was merely expressing her personal disagreement and asked why she should not be allowed to express her opinion. He then took issue with Mohanlal saying that society has accepted Adhila and Noora, questioning whether society really “accepted” them, and arguing that, even if that’s the case, acceptance does not mean people are no longer allowed to question them. But this is where the language of “just an opinion” becomes misleading. People can, of course, hold different personal, cultural, or religious views and biases. But that is markedly different from asking whether same-sex relationships should be treated as legitimate or acceptable in public life, because such attitudes do not exist in a vacuum. Research has linked stigma and discrimination against sexual minorities to poorer mental-health outcomes, while major professional and scientific bodies, including the American Psychological Association (APA), have documented how prejudice, discrimination, harassment, and violence can affect the wellbeing and safety of LGBTQIA+ people. This is especially worth noting because UA itself has repeatedly invoked the APA as an authoritative source while using its work to support the channel’s arguments about sexualisation, clothing, and the fashion industry. In his debate with Darsana, Ameer even asked, “Is there a bigger authority than APA in the field of psychology?” The APA, notably, has also published guidelines on psychological practice with sexual minorities that explicitly state that sexual-minority orientations are not mental illnesses, caution against attempts to change them, and discuss the importance of recognising the discrimination faced by sexual minorities. That guidance, however, does not seem to appeal to UA and finds no mention in their videos. So while the channel is quite assertive in invoking the APA’s authority when citing studies on sexualisation, it quietly ignores the same institution’s guidelines when discussing queer lives. The general argument in UA’s video on Bigg Boss went roughly like this: showing a same-sex couple on a mainstream reality show amounts to “normalisation”. The video compared this to showing alcohol consumption on television until drinking becomes something viewers see as ordinary. Hilal then argued that children exposed to such “normalisation” could be confused because their prefrontal cortex (front part of the brain) is not yet fully developed. He connected this to “studies about gender dysphoria”, citing a figure of around 27% of adolescents who, he says, experience some form of gender-related confusion “in New York or somewhere.” Gender dysphoria, for context, is a scientific term used to describe the significant distress some people may experience when their gender identity does not align with the sex they were assigned at birth. Basically, UA’s argument was that because adolescents’ brains are still developing, exposure to same-sex relationships or gender-related content could confuse them about their sexuality or gender. The 27% figure appears to come from a real 2017 Williams Institute study based on a California Health Interview Survey, but the study says something very different from what Hilal described. It found that 27% of California teenagers aged 12 to 17 were “viewed by people at school” as “gender non-conforming.” That did not mean they had gender dysphoria. It was based on a question about how other people perceived their gender expression — essentially, whether their appearance or style was seen as more masculine or feminine than expected for their sex. It was neither a clinical diagnosis, a measure of gender identity, nor a study of adolescents in New York. The comparison with alcohol also falls flat. While studies do say media representation can influence what people see as familiar or socially acceptable, that does not mean everything represented on television is something viewers can “pick up”. Drinking is a behaviour, while sexual orientation is not. Seeing other people drink may influence how someone thinks about drinking, but there is no equivalent evidence that seeing a same-sex couple causes someone to develop same-sex attraction. In fact, there is evidence to the contrary. A good example is the 2013 paper Same-Sex Sexual Attraction Does Not Spread in Adolescent Social Networks — a longitudinal study of more than 14,000 adolescents. The results have suggested that peer influence had little effect on whether adolescents developed heterosexual or homosexual attraction. More importantly, there is another side to the question of what happens when queer people become visible on television. Representation can make people who have rarely seen themselves reflected in mainstream media more visible to the wider public, and can give queer viewers a sense that their experiences are not unusual or unknowable. When Bigg Boss Malayalam featured openly queer contestants in 2022, TNM spoke to queer activists and participants who described the visibility as significant precisely because many people in Kerala had little exposure to openly queer lives. One contestant, Ashwin Vijay, told TNM that seeing other queer people on the show helped him feel comfortable enough to come out, while another activist said that people around him began to understand that “there are people like us coexisting with them.” UA, however, treats even this kind of visibility with explicit suspicion. In another video, from a campus debate at Mambad MES College, Basil moved from questioning the “normalisation” of homosexuality to arguing that homosexuality itself can be “cured”. He pointed to what he called “ex-gay communities” in the West and said, “No one can say it cannot be cured,” arguing that the question is only how much of it can be cured. Basil speaks during a campus debate on atheism and liberalism at Government Engineering College, Thrissur, on September 5, 2023. He then drew a distinction between feeling same-sex attraction and acting on it — “You can feel gay, but the sin is in acting on that feeling” — before placing homosexuality alongside paedophilia, incest, necrophilia, and bestiality. Allowing homosexual people to “live their life”, he warned, would lead to “anarchy”. The first claim here, that homosexuality can be cured, has no support from the mainstream scientific and medical evidence UA otherwise invokes. The APA’s review of sexual-orientation change efforts concluded that such efforts are unlikely to be successful and involve a risk of harm. Its subsequent policy resolution says scientific evidence and clinical experience indicate that sexual-orientation change efforts put people at significant risk of harm. The APA likewise says that homosexuality is not a mental illness and that conversion therapy is not a legitimate therapeutic treatment. That does not mean there have never been people who say they changed their sexual orientation, or who identify as “ex-gay”. It means those accounts are not evidence that sexual orientation can be reliably changed through a therapeutic or religious intervention. The APA's review notes that people may report changes in behaviour or identity without evidence that their underlying sexual attractions have changed; efforts to change their orientation can also encourage people to conceal them. In other words, the existence of communities that say they have changed is not itself evidence that a “cure” exists. The comparison with paedophilia, incest, necrophilia, and bestiality also collapses fundamentally different categories. The World Health Organisation removed homosexuality from its classification of mental disorders decades ago, and notes that sexual orientation itself is not a disorder. By contrast, psychiatric classifications distinguish between unusual sexual interests and conditions that involve significant distress or impairment, cause harm, or involve people who cannot or do not consent. Paedophilia, for example, involves sexual interest in children, who cannot legally consent to sexual activity with adults. That is fundamentally different from a consensual sexual or romantic relationship between two adults of the same sex. In the video, Basil's argument moved from “some sexual feelings should not be acted upon” — a proposition that is hardly controversial — to treating homosexuality itself as something morally or medically comparable to sexual interests involving people/animals who cannot consent. The fact that a person can have a feeling without acting on it does not make every kind of feeling equivalent, any more than the existence of consent makes every relationship morally identical. What matters in a consensual adult relationship is that the people involved are capable of consent and are choosing to participate. What the response to UA says Problematic as they are, these arguments do not remain confined to UA’s videos. They can be taken up and weaponised by those seeking to discredit feminism, queer rights, and atheism, with the authority of scientific research lending their attacks a veneer of objectivity. Aysha Mahmood, a social activist who has followed and critiqued the channel since its early days on Clubhouse, says UA has increasingly become a source of such arguments for the wider manosphere. “I have often noticed how they have become the anchor and source for the manosphere to attack feminists, queer persons, and atheists with ‘science-backed’ claims,” she told TNM. For Aysha, there is also a contradiction in the authority these arguments derive from their speakers’ professional credentials. UA’s speakers include doctors, dentists, teachers, and educators, she noted, even as some of the positions they advance involve gender segregation and attempts to change sexual orientation. One of the more interesting aspects of the Unmasking Anomalies channel is that its audience is not necessarily judging whether the research holds up. They’re often responding to the performance of expertise itself — to the confidence of someone who clearly seems to have “done the reading”. They respond to the speed and fluency with which a speaker produces a study, a statistic, or the name of a researcher in the middle of an argument. The sheer number of citations can itself become a sign of victory. Three papers mentioned in 90 seconds can sound more convincing than one carefully explained paper, even when none of the three quite says what the speaker claims it does. In the comments we examined, the praise often centred on exactly that. Speakers were admired for being able to produce a citation quickly and calmly while their feminist or queer interlocutors are still making a moral or personal argument. An opponent was described as having been “destroyed” or “silenced” because she could not immediately produce a counterpoint for a study cited. Darsana described this as a form of “scientific misogyny” — the use of scientific language and research to give anti-feminist claims an authority they might not otherwise have. She said what struck her was how, at the same time as UA was presenting its arguments as scientific, feminism was being repeatedly characterised as emotional, irrational, and insufficiently evidence-based. Comments on Unmasking Anomalies videos reveal how viewers reward the appearance of scientific authority: praising speakers for their command of research and facts, while dismissing opposing arguments as emotional, uninformed, or lacking intelligence. Even when she approached UA for her debate with Ameer, she said, they asked about her educational qualifications and told her that previous “Instagram feminists” had brought down the quality of their debates because they made emotional arguments rather than evidence-based ones. “For us, these issues are personal, and it's about women's bodies, so women would obviously be angry about what is said,” Darsana pointed out. The channel, however, uses this emotionality to its own end, framing the narrative such that their own side is occupying the position of science, while the other is asked to prove that it is even capable of reasoning. It is a particularly effective rhetorical position because it asks the audience to make a judgement before they have had a chance to examine the evidence. Ameer’s two-and-a-half-hour debate with Darsana is unusual for UA in that sense, precisely because it gave Darsana time to return to the studies, question what they actually said, and ask where the missing steps in the argument came from. This is the video where several of UA’s citations that sounded authoritative in the original debate begin to look much less conclusive. Interestingly, the comments under this video also seem to reflect a different kind of response to the opposing debater. There is a visible degree of respect for Darsana’s ability to argue her position and push back on the citations, which is a small but telling contrast to the more combative reaction often seen in the channel’s shorter debate videos. Some viewers, she said, seemed surprised that a woman could read academic papers, reason logically, and “speak their language”. “It was disappointing to see that,” she told us. “But it also made me think there was something I did that made them think slightly differently.” Of course, none of this is evidence that UA's speakers are aware their citations don't hold up and use them regardless. But what's harder to write off as an accident is the consistency with which this happens. Across the six-plus videos we watched, the same seven or eight sources seem to be doing the same work, arriving at a recommendation about why women should be policed, while rarely at one asking men, specifically, to do anything differently. The question, then, is not whether science has anything to say about sexual violence, attraction, gender, or human behaviour, because of course it does. The question is what happens when someone uses the authority of science to make social restrictions appear inevitable for one section of society. And that would definitely need some unmasking. TNM has reached out to Abdulla Basil CP with questions. The story will be updated if and when he responds.

articles.title: Chennai: 71.24 kg heroin worth Rs 140 crore seized from ice cream vending vehicle
articles.summary: The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) seized around 71.24 kg of heroin, worth Rs 140 crore, from an ice cream vending vehicle near Madhavaram in Chennai on Tuesday, November 17. Two men have been arrested in connection with the seizure and remanded to judicial custody. The accused have been identified as Abdul Shukkur (32) and his brother-in-law Shafiq Ahmed (30), both natives of southern Tamil Nadu who were residing in Chennai. According to reports, the DRI received specific intelligence inputs on Monday night about a large consignment of narcotics being smuggled from abroad and being transported through vehicles in Chennai suburbs. Following the tip-off, special teams were formed and surveillance was intensified near Chennai airport and along the Chennai-Tiruchy and Chennai-Kolkata National Highways. On Tuesday, DRI officials spotted an ice cream vending vehicle parked near an ice manufacturing factory in Madhavaram, along the Chennai-Kolkata National Highway. The vehicle was reportedly waiting to load ice from the factory. During a search of the vehicle, officials found several packets of heroin stacked inside its freezing unit and hidden among the racks used to store ice cream. The officials subsequently arrested the two men who were inside the vehicle. Officials suspect that an international drug trafficking network had engaged them to move the narcotics using the ice cream vehicle as cover, believing that such a vehicle would be less likely to attract checks from the police and anti-narcotics agencies. The two men were produced before the court in Alandur on November 18 and remanded to judicial custody. Reacting to the seizure, former Chief Minister and Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) president MK Stalin alleged that the deterioration of law and order under the TVK government, along with alleged sexual misconduct by ruling party functionaries, robberies, burglaries and custodial deaths, had turned Tamil Nadu into a “vice city”. “The DGP may say that a case has been registered. But he should explain why the state police have been unable to arrest drug traffickers. What happened to the 65 units formed to prevent drug use and trafficking in the state? Chief Minister Vijay holds the Home portfolio. If he is not prepared to offer an explanation now, when will he do so?” Stalin asked.
